A BSTRACT Humanoid vision–language–action (VLA) models translate multimodal task un- derstanding into coordinated whole-body behavior. Existing approaches equip pretrained vision–language or video generation backbones with action experts, but their pretraining does not directly establish whole-body motion priors. Uni- fied or upper–lower-body action designs also lack dedicated root, body, and hand modeling despite their distinct requirements. These limitations increase the bur- den of learning precise, coordinated actions from limited task-specific humanoid demonstrations. We introduce Kimodo-Policy, which initializes visually grounded control with pretrained text-to-motion (T2M) priors over inter-joint coordination and temporal structure. Its three-stage root–body–hand architecture combines dedicated generators with explicit dependencies: root trajectories condition body generation, while future body features and visual observations guide hand con- trol. We pretrain the policy on diverse humanoid demonstrations, conditioning actions on visual observations, language instructions, and motion history. With 678M total and only 92M trainable parameters, Kimodo-Policy achieves strong performance on HumanoidArena, SIMPLE, and real-world loco-manipulation tasks. Further experiments show performance gains from larger VLA pretrain- ing datasets, greater model capacity, and stronger pretrained T2M priors. 1 Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027 054 055 056 057 058 059 060 061 062 063 064 065 066 067 068 069 070 071 072 073 074 075 076 077 078 079 080 081 082 083 084 085 086 087 088 089 090 1 I NTRODUCTION Vision–language–action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and ac- tion generation across manipulation tasks and robot embodiments (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026b; 2025). Learning instruction-conditioned behaviors from demonstrations provides a unified mapping from multimodal inputs to robot actions. Extending VLA learning to humanoids could broaden task coverage in human environments, where locomo- tion, posture, and manipulation must be coordinated (Bjorck et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026a; Hu et al., 2026). For example, transferring objects between tables requires grasping, turning, walking, and placement while maintaining balance (Fig. 1, bottom). Such tasks require grounding task in- tent and visual feedback in coherent whole-body actions, motivating the extension of robot policy architectures to humanoid loco-manipulation. Humanoid policy learning commonly extends the backbone–action expert paradigm from manipula- tion to whole-body control. Pretrained vision–language models encode instruction and observation semantics (Fig. 2(a)) (Bjorck et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026a; Hu et al., 2026), while video gen- erators supply spatiotemporal priors for scene evolution (Fig. 2(b)) (Zheng et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). These representations condition action generation across root, body, and hand motion. Uni- fied predictors generate whole-body sequences (Fig. 2(d)) (Hu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026); hybrid designs combine upper-body joint targets with lower-body locomotion commands executed by dedicated controllers (Fig. 2(e)) (Zhong et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025). The former captures cross-component dependencies; the latter couples upper-body control with learned locomotion and stabilization. Both transfer pretrained semantic and visual dynamics knowledge to humanoid loco- manipulation. Despite these advances, two challenges remain. ❶ Insufficient Whole-Body Motion Priors. Com- pared with fixed-base manipulation, humanoid control requires higher-dimensional inter-joint and temporal coordination. Backbone pretraining (Bjorck et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026a; Zheng et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026) does not directly equip action generators with priors aligned with target hu- manoid kinematics, leaving them to learn these priors, often from limited task-specific demonstra- tions. ❷ Insufficient Differentiation of Motion Components. Root, body, and hand control differ in scale and precision. Unified prediction (Hu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026) may create competing objectives; hybrid execution (Zhong et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025) does not itself provide dedicated root, body, and hand generators. Both must accommodate component-specific requirements while maintaining whole-body coordination. Recent text-to-motion (T2M) methods learn structured motion distributions conditioned on text or spatial constraints (Petrovich et al., 2022; Tevet et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023a; Guo et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024). Building on these advances, Kimodo-Policy combines a pre- 091 092 093 094 095 096 097 098 099 100 101 102 103 104 105 106 107 Figure 2: Comparison of Humanoid Policy Architectures. We transfer Kimodo’s pretrained inter-joint and temporal priors to high-dimensional, visually grounded control (Fig. 2(c)) (Rempe et al., 2026), easing mo- tion learning from limited task-specific humanoid demonstrations. ❷ Strong Component-Specific Motion Modeling. Dedicated generators (Fig. 2(f)) predict root translation and heading, root- conditioned body motion, and hand controls conditioned on future body features and visual ob- servations. Their dependencies support component specialization and whole-body coordination. We pretrain on diverse humanoid demonstrations to generate actions conditioned on visual observa- tions, language instructions, and motion history. With 678M total and only 92M trainable param- eters, Kimodo-Policy shows consistent gains from more VLA pretraining data, larger models, and stronger T2M priors. Our main contributions are: • We introduce Kimodo-Policy, a humanoid VLA framework transferring pretrained T2M priors to whole-body control. Pretraining on diverse humanoid demonstrations conditions closed-loop actions on visual observations, language instructions, and motion history. 122 123 124 125 126 127 128 129 130 131 132 133 134 135 136 137 138 139 140 141 142 143 144 145 146 147 148 149 150 151 152 153 154 155 156 157 158 159 160 161 • We propose dedicated root, body, and hand generators in a three-stage architecture to meet distinct control requirements. Explicit cross-stage conditioning preserves motion depen- dencies, supporting specialized motion generation and coordinated whole-body control. • We demonstrate strong performance on HumanoidArena, SIMPLE, and real-world hu- manoid tasks using 678M parameters (only 92M trainable), with consistent gains from larger VLA pretraining datasets, greater model capacity, and stronger T2M priors. 2 R ELATED W ORK 2.1 H UMANOID V ISION -L ANGUAGE -A CTION M ODELS Humanoid VLA models typically use pretrained vision–language models (VLMs) or video genera- tion models (VGMs). VLM-based methods transfer visual-semantic knowledge to actions (Bjorck et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026a; Zhong et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026): GR00T N1 (Bjorck et al., 2025) couples a VLM with a diffusion action model, while Ψ 0 (Wei et al., 2026a) transfers representa- tions from human egocentric demonstrations to a humanoid action expert. VGM-based methods exploit visual dynamics priors (Zheng et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026): MotionWAM (Zheng et al., 2026) generates whole-body motion from intermediate video features; WholeBodyWAM (Li et al., 2026) grounds world–action priors in whole-body controllers. Unified generators (Hu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026) share prediction across motion components; hybrids (Zhong et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025) combine upper-body targets with locomotion commands. HAF (Gu et al., 2026) stages generation with a shared action expert, expanding the active action set and refining earlier predic- tions. Kimodo-Policy instead transfers a T2M backbone with pretrained inter-joint and temporal priors, reducing the need to learn motion regularities from humanoid demonstrations. Dedicated root, body, and hand generators meet distinct control requirements, while cross-stage conditioning supports coordinated, visually grounded whole-body behavior. 2.2 T EXT - TO -M OTION (T2M) T2M includes TEMOS’s variational language–motion modeling (Petrovich et al., 2022), pose-space MDM (Tevet et al., 2023) and latent-space MLD (Chen et al., 2023) diffusion, and autoregressive T2M-GPT (Zhang et al., 2023a) and masked MoMask (Guo et al., 2024) quantized token generation. OmniControl (Xie et al., 2024) adds spatial constraints; Kimodo (Rempe et al., 2026) trains con- trollable root–body diffusion hierarchies at scale for human and humanoid skeletons. Humanoid- VLA (Ding et al., 2025) and ZeroWBC (Yang et al., 2026) learn autoregressive motion priors in pretrained language models and VLMs, respectively, before visual integration or task adaptation. MotionWAM (Zheng et al., 2026) adapts a pretrained video world model via staged video–motion training; WholeBodyWAM (Zhang et al., 2026) integrates a pretrained motion expert with video and action experts. Kimodo-Policy directly reuses a diffusion T2M backbone pretrained at scale in robot kinematic space. Dedicated root–body–hand generators ground inter-joint and temporal pri- ors in vision and motion history for closed-loop loco-manipulation, reducing relearning from robot demonstrations while accommodating distinct control requirements. 3 Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027 162 163 3 164 165 166 167 168 169 Kimodo-Policy adapts Kimodo’s pretrained motion prior for visually grounded, closed-loop hu- manoid control. We describe its root–body–hand architecture and visual conditioning (Sec. 3.1), motion-prior transfer and history-conditioned control (Sec. 3.2), and training and inference (Sec. 3.3). Background on Kimodo and ControlNet is provided in Appendix A. We formulate language-conditioned humanoid loco-manipulation as closed-loop prediction of short action chunks. At step k, the policy receives instruction ℓ, the current egocentric RGB image I k , available motion history H k = [x k−L+1 , . . . , x k ] in Kimodo’s represen- tation, and the current bilateral hand state s hk . It predicts a K-frame chunk, with a i = [r i , b i , h i ] encoding root motion, articulated body motion, and bilateral hand controls: 199 200 201 202 203 A k+1:k+K ∼ π θ ( · | I k , ℓ, H k , s hk ). 204 205 206 207 208 209 210 211 212 213 214 215 (1) Root and body outputs provide kinematic references to a low-level motion tracker (Ze et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2026), while hand outputs specify synchronized binary or continuous closure com- mands according to the task interface. A chunk prefix is executed before replanning from updated observations, combining visual feedback with temporal context from observed history. Three-Stage Architecture. As shown in Figure 3, Kimodo-Policy extends Kimodo’s (Rempe et al., 2026) pretrained generator with dedicated root, body, and hand stages. LLM2Vec (BehnamGhader et al., 2024) encodes instructions; frozen DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) extracts visual features. Trainable ControlNet-Root and ControlNet-Body inject these features via Dual-Path Fusion into their corresponding frozen Kimodo denoisers, which also condition on instruction embeddings and motion history. The root stage predicts global translation and heading; their local representation conditions articulated body generation. Trainable HandNet predicts bilateral hand controls from fu- ture body features, visual features, and the current bilateral hand state. All root-to-body conditioning is detached, blocking body-stage gradients to Kimodo-Root and ControlNet-Root. HandNet’s body and visual inputs are also detached, so hand supervision cannot update Kimodo-Body or either Con- trolNet branch. These boundaries isolate stage optimization while preserving forward dependencies. Root–body predictions yield whole-body tracking references executed with hand commands. 4 Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027 216 217 218 219 220 221 222 223 224 225 226 227 228 229 230 231 232 233 234 235 236 237 238 239 240 241 242 243 244 245 246 Dual-Path Fusion. DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) encodes the current egocentric image into spa- tial tokens for trainable root and body ControlNet branches. At selected layers of each Kimodo denoiser, future-motion hidden states query these tokens through cross-attention, while a token- axis MLP maps the image-token sequence to the future temporal horizon. Summed outputs pass through a layer-specific zero-initialized projection, producing a residual hint for the corresponding Kimodo layer. Hints are added only to future-motion tokens, leaving the constrained history prefix unchanged. Zero initialization preserves pretrained behavior at adaptation onset; both paths ground the frozen prior through content-selective visual retrieval and temporally aligned conditioning. HandNet. Hand control specifies opening or closing rather than kinematic pose trajectories, moti- vating a dedicated bilateral diffusion head. At each denoising step, HandNet jointly processes the current hand state, noisy future hand controls, future body hidden states, and visual tokens to predict two hand-control values per future frame. Conditioning on predicted body features and the current scene aligns hand commands with whole-body action, while the separate head keeps hand labels outside the root–body motion space. It supports binary open/close states and continuous closure changes. During training, body and visual features are detached: hand supervision updates HandNet without gradients to the motion denoiser or ControlNet. 3.2 A DAPTING M OTION P RIORS FOR C LOSED -L OOP C ONTROL Motion Prior Transfer. Figure 4 illustrates how a pretrained motion prior supplies temporal struc- ture and whole-body coordination for visually grounded control. Given only “Sit on the sofa,” Ki- modo (Rempe et al., 2026) generates a coherent sequence ending in a seated posture (top), but lacks grounding in the current scene and robot state. Kimodo-Policy freezes this backbone and injects egocentric visual features through trainable ControlNet branches; motion-history constraints anchor predictions to the ongoing trajectory, enabling the same task from visual observations and state his- tory (bottom). Task-specific learning thus adapts reusable behavior-level structure to the instruction, scene, and state, reducing the need to relearn basic motion patterns from robot demonstrations while preserving coherent closed-loop execution. 247 248 249 250 251 252 253 254 255 256 257 258 259 260 261 262 263 264 265 266 267 268 269 Figure 4: Motion-Prior Transfer. Top: frozen Kimodo generates a complete “Sit on the sofa” sequence from text. Bottom: Kimodo-Policy predicts short chunks from vision and motion history for closed-loop control. Light brown: observed history; blue: predicted and executed motion. Motion-History Conditioning. Fixed T2M sequences cannot respond to deviations between pre- dicted and measured motion or scene changes. We therefore formulate each closed-loop query as constrained motion completion in Kimodo’s kinematic representation. Observed history forms the prefix of a history–future window, with feature-wise masks identifying available kinematic values. The prefix is restored before each denoising step; the unconstrained future becomes the next ac- tion chunk. Trainable ControlNet branches inject current egocentric image features into Kimodo’s root and body denoisers, grounding predictions while retaining the pretrained root–body structure. The tracker executes a chunk prefix; updated history and images condition the next query. This receding-horizon loop preserves the motion prior with continual visual and state-based correction. 5 Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027 270 271 3.3 272 273 274 275 276 277 Training Objective. ControlNet branches and HandNet denoise demonstration windows. At sam- pled diffusion timesteps, Gaussian noise perturbs normalized root–body features and hand targets; feature-wise masks constrain observed history, with supervision on valid future frames: (︁ )︁ L = λ r L r + λ b L b + λ h L h + λ ∆ L ∆ , (2) The masked MSE terms L r , L b , and L h reconstruct clean normalized root–body features and hand targets. Binary hand targets use [−1, 1]; continuous targets encode closure residuals from the latest valid observed hand state. L ∆ computes ℓ 1 error in predicted versus demonstrated consecutive hand-control changes, including the observed-to-first-future transition; continuous residuals are first converted to closure values. All losses mask padding; hand losses also mask unavailable labels, and transitions require two valid adjacent labels. The main MSE weights are (λ r , λ b , λ h , λ ∆ ) = (4, 1, 1, 0.2). Predicted root motion and, in the main configuration, root ControlNet features are detached before body generation; HandNet receives detached body and visual features. Kimodo denoisers and the DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) encoder remain frozen. 278 279 280 281 282 283 284 285 286 287 288 289 290 291 292 293 294 295 296 297 298 299 300 301 302 303 304 305 306 307 308 309 310 311 312 313 314 315 316 317 318 319 320 321 322 323 T RAINING AND I NFERENCE Inference. Each policy query encodes the language instruction and current egocentric image, and represents available proprioceptive history in Kimodo’s motion space with frame- and feature-wise observation masks. DDIM (Song et al., 2021) iteratively denoises future motion and hand sequences initialized from Gaussian noise. Each step restores observed history, injects visual features into frozen root and body denoisers via ControlNet, conditions body generation on predicted root mo- tion, and predicts hand controls with HandNet using the current hand state, visual features, and future body features. After denoising, we invert the motion representation and map root and joint trajectories, together with bilateral hand commands, to tracker-compatible references. The low-level whole-body tracker executes a chunk prefix; the policy replans from updated images and proprio- ceptive states, combining structured motion generation with continual closed-loop correction. 4 E XPERIMENTAL R ESULTS We evaluate Kimodo-Policy through single- and multi-task HumanoidArena control (Sec. 4.1), SIM- PLE manipulation (Sec. 4.2), and real-world deployment (Sec. 4.3). Analyses cover T2M backbone quality (Sec. 4.4), data and model scaling (Sec. 4.5), and design ablations (Sec. 4.6). Appendix B details the datasets, training protocols, and evaluation environments. 4.1 E VALUATION ON THE H UMANOID A RENA B ENCHMARK HumanoidArena (Wang et al., 2026a) covers seven language-conditioned tasks spanning human– object interaction (HOI) and human–scene interaction (HSI). We evaluate independent per-task fine- tuning and joint training across SONIC tasks. Appendix C.1 (Fig. 11) visualizes the tasks. Single-task results. We fine-tune one policy per task with RTC disabled to match baselines. Kimodo-Policy uses direct task fine-tuning; Kimodo-Policy ∗ initializes ControlNet and the hand head from our 419-hour VLA pretraining. Kimodo-Policy achieves the highest overall success rate (SR; 69.51%), exceeding the strongest baseline, DP (Chi et al., 2023) (60.0%), by 9.51 percentage points. It also leads in average HSI SR (84.58%) and ties Kimodo-Policy ∗ for lowest average fall rate (AFR; 4.29%). Kimodo-Policy ∗ achieves 67.14% overall and 84.17% average HSI SR, leading OpenDoor (93.3%) and VisNavi (76.7%). We fine-tune an independent policy for each of the eight benchmark tasks and report the results in Table 3. This protocol isolates skill acquisition while testing robustness under increasing distribution shifts. See Appendix C.2 (Fig. 12) for task visualizations. Single-task results. Table 3 evaluates VLA-pretrained Kimodo-Policy (Ours ∗ ) on eight SIMPLE tasks, aggregating L0–L2 success rates with RTC disabled to match the baselines. It achieves best or joint-best results on six tasks: Handover (83% vs. 80% for the strongest baseline), Mobile P&P (70% vs. 60%), OpenOven (57% vs. 53%), OpenFaucet (53% vs. 33%), CloseDoor and Push Office Chair (both 100%, tied with Ψ 0 ). It ranks second on XMoveBendPick (80% vs. 93% for Ψ 0 ) and OpenTrashCan (63% vs. 83%). Without VLA pretraining, Kimodo-Policy achieves 51.67% mean success; re- moving the T2M backbone, unfreezing it, replacing MSE with Kimodo’s original motion objective, or removing root–body gradient detachment yields 18.33%, 31.67%, 35.00%, or 45.00%, respec- tively. These results support a frozen motion prior, MSE supervision, and gradient separation. VLA pretraining raises success from 51.67% to 56.11%, with generally lower and less variable training loss. Both retain the T2M backbone, indicating complementary benefits (Appendix F). 5 C ONCLUSION Kimodo-Policy adapts pretrained text-to-motion priors for visually grounded, closed-loop humanoid control through root–body–hand generation and continual visual and state feedback. Experiments show strong results on HumanoidArena, SIMPLE, and eight real-world tasks with 92M trainable parameters out of 678M total. Stronger priors, more VLA data, and greater capacity improve per- formance within the evaluated settings. A.2). 710 711 712 713 714 715 716 717 718 719 720 721 722 723 724 725 726 727 728 729 730 731 732 733 734 735 736 737 738 739 740 741 742 743 744 745 746 747 748 749 750 751 752 753 754 755 A.1 P RELIMINARIES K IMODO Architecture Overview. Kimodo (Rempe et al., 2026) is a framework for controllable kinematic motion generation based on diffusion, with pretrained models for both the SOMA (Saito et al., 2026) human skeleton and the Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Starting from Gaussian noise, it generates motion sequences conditioned on text prompts and optional kinematic constraints using a two-stage Transformer denoiser operating on pose tokens. At each diffusion step t, its input–output mapping is summarized as ˆ︁ 0 = D θ (X t , c, t) = [ R ˆ︁ 0 , B ˆ︁ 0 ]. X (3) ˆ︁ 0 and B ˆ︁ 0 are the Here, X t is the noisy motion, c collects the text and motion conditions, and R predicted clean root and body motions. The denoiser first predicts the global root motion, then uses its local representation to condition body prediction. Text embeddings provide semantic guidance, while masked motion constraints support control through keyframes, joint positions and orientations, and root waypoints or paths. In this work, we primarily use the Kimodo-G1 motion generation model as our pretrained backbone, which is trained on human motion-capture data retargeted to the G1 skeleton using the SOMA retargeter to enable direct generation of kinematic robot motions. Motion Representation. Kimodo (Rempe et al., 2026) encodes a motion sequence as X = [x 1 , . . . , x N ] for N frames, with the root at the first frame centered horizontally at the origin. For a skeleton with J joints, each frame contains six groups of kinematic features: x n = [r pn , r an , j pn , j vn , j an , f n ] ∈ R 12J+9 . (4) Here, r pn ∈ R 3 is the global root position obtained by smoothing the horizontal (x, z) coordinates of the pelvis while preserving its vertical height, and r an = [cos ψ n , sin ψ n ] ∈ R 2 encodes the global heading angle ψ n . Joint positions j pn ∈ R 3J use horizontal offsets from the smoothed root and absolute vertical coordinates, with axes aligned to the world frame. Joint velocities j vn ∈ R 3J are computed from global joint positions, and joint rotations j an ∈ R 6J encode each joint’s global orientation using a continuous 6D representation. The binary vector f n ∈ {0, 1} 4 records contact states for the left heel, left toe, right heel, and right toe. These features form a root component = [r pn , r an ] and a body component b n = [j pn , j vn , j an , f n ], providing an explicit decomposition r glob n for root and body motion prediction while supporting spatial constraints on root trajectories, joint positions, and joint orientations. A.2 C ONTROL N ET Architecture Overview. ControlNet (Zhang et al., 2023b) adapts a pretrained diffusion model to new spatial or semantic conditions while preserving the capabilities acquired by its original back- bone. Its central design freezes the pretrained denoiser and adds a trainable control branch with a structurally aligned sequence of layers. The control branch processes the additional condition and produces intermediate features that are injected into the corresponding layers of the frozen branch through zero-initialized projections. For a frozen layer F ℓ , a trainable control layer G ϕ,ℓ , and con- dition representation c, the interaction can be written as (︁ )︁ ctrl lock h ctrl h lock ) + Z ℓ h ctrl (5) ℓ+1 = G ϕ,ℓ (h ℓ , c), ℓ+1 = F ℓ (h ℓ ℓ+1 , where Z ℓ is a learnable 1×1 projection initialized to zero. At initialization, the residual path there- fore contributes no signal and the adapted model exactly follows the pretrained denoiser. During optimization, gradients update only the control branch and zero projections, allowing the model to learn condition-specific behavior while retaining the original generative prior. This structure is particularly useful when the target dataset is limited or when preserving the motion regularities of a pretrained generator is important. In Kimodo-Policy, we adopt this principle for a transformer-based 14 Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027 756 757 758 759 760 761 762 763 764 765 766 767 768 769 770 771 772 773 774 775 776 777 778 779 780 781 782 783 784 785 786 motion denoiser rather than a convolutional image U-Net (Ronneberger et al., 2015). The frozen Ki- modo root and body denoisers provide the motion prior, while trainable ControlNet branches receive visual features and inject residual hints at selected denoising layers. The specific visual encoder, dual-path fusion mechanism, and root/body injection strategy are described in Sec. 3.1. B E XPERIMENTAL S ETUP This section describes the data, training protocols, and evaluation environments used to assess Kimodo-Policy. We first detail VLA policy pretraining on heterogeneous humanoid demonstrations (Sec. B.1), and then describe post-training and evaluation on the HumanoidArena and SIMPLE simulators as well as on a physical humanoid robot (Sec. B.2). B.1 P RETRAINING Dataset. We assemble a 419-hour pretraining corpus from three publicly released humanoid datasets (Fig. 9). HIW-500 provides teleoperated Unitree G1 demonstrations collected in real homes. From UniFoLM-WBT, we use the 14 task-specific G1 subsets available when our corpus was assembled: the BrainCo subsets Collect Plates into Dishwasher, Make the Bed, Pick Up Medicine, and Pickup Pillow; the Dex1 subset Put Clothes into Washing Machine; and the Inspire subsets Clean the Liv- ing Room, Collect Clothes (MainCamOnly), Pick Up Drinks, Pickup Pillow (MainCamOnly), Put Clothes into Basket, Put Clothes into Washing Machine, Put Clothes into Washing Machine (Main- CamOnly), Put Drinks into Fridge, and Put Vegetables into Basket. Main-camera-only variants are included when available, while UniFoLM-WBT entries released after this snapshot are excluded. Humanoid Everyday (Zhao et al., 2025) contributes 10.3K trajectories, over three million frames, and 260 tasks spanning dexterous manipulation, articulated-object interaction, human–robot inter- action, and locomotion-integrated behaviors. We form training examples from an egocentric image, a language instruction, a 100-frame motion history, and a 50-frame future action chunk sampled at 30 Hz, converting trajectories to Kimodo’s motion representation. 787 788 789 790 791 792 793 794 795 796 797 798 799 800 801 802 803 804 805 806 807 808 809 Figure 9: Composition of the VLA Pretraining Corpus. The corpus combines HIW-500, 14 task subsets from UniFoLM-WBT available when the corpus was assembled, and Humanoid Everyday. UniFoLM-WBT entries released after corpus construction are excluded. Implementation Details. We pretrain the policy for 1,000k optimization steps on 16 NVIDIA H200 GPUs, taking approximately 60 hours with bfloat16 mixed precision and a global batch size of 1024. During VLA pretraining, hand supervision is represented as a two-dimensional binary vector indicating the open/closed state of the left and right hands. This shared representation accommodates the different hand morphologies, degrees of freedom, and control conventions in the source datasets, preserving grasp-and-release semantics while providing a consistent target for the hand head. We use AdamW with learning rates of 3 × 10 −5 for the ControlNet backbone and 1 × 10 −4 for the 15 Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027 810 811 812 813 814 815 816 817 818 819 820 821 822 823 824 825 826 827 828 829 830 831 832 833 834 835 836 837 838 839 840 841 842 843 844 845 846 ControlNet adapters and hand head, together with a weight decay of 0.01. The learning rate follows a cosine schedule with 1% warm-up and a minimum of 10% of its initial value. B.2 P OST -T RAINING HumanoidArena Benchmark. HumanoidArena (Wang et al., 2026a; Luo et al., 2026) provides seven leg-critical tasks: three human–object and four human–scene interaction tasks requiring co- ordinated locomotion, balance, posture adjustment, and manipulation. Its SONIC data contain 100 successful demonstrations per task (700 total) with synchronized egocentric RGB, proprioceptive states, and whole-body targets. We use all seven tasks for single-task fine-tuning and joint multi-task training, the latter being more challenging because one policy must acquire all tasks simultaneously. We evaluate closed-loop performance with SONIC using success rate (SR) and average fall rate (AFR), capturing both task completion and stability during whole-body task execution. SIMPLE Benchmark. SIMPLE (Wei et al., 2026b) integrates MuJoCo contact dynamics with Isaac Sim rendering for scalable evaluation of humanoid loco-manipulation. The paper describes a benchmark comprising 60 tasks; of these, 18 have been released in the public codebase to date. The paper reports baseline results for six tasks, with two evaluated using AMO and four using the SONIC tracker. From the currently released tasks, we select eight for evaluation: Handover, Mobile P&P, XMoveBendPick, CloseDoor, OpenOven, OpenFaucet, Push Office Chair, and OpenTrashCan. Together, these tasks cover object handover, mobile pick-and-place, articulated-object interaction, and household-object manipulation, allowing us to assess policy robustness and execution stability in contact-rich whole-body control. Real-World Data Collection and Setup. We collect real-world demonstrations with a teleopera- tion system implemented on top of and extended from the NVIDIA Isaac-GR00T data-preparation pipeline (Bjorck et al., 2025). As shown on the left of Fig. 10, the operator uses a PICO 4 Ultra head- set and hand controllers together with PICO body trackers for whole-body and lower-limb tracking. The humanoid is equipped with an Intel RealSense D435i camera and Dex3-1 dexterous hands. We define eight real-world tasks spanning locomotion, balance, and single- and dual-arm manipulation, and record 25–30 demonstrations per task. The two plots on the right of Fig. 10 show representative joint-position traces from two of these tasks: in Football Scoring (Fig. 10a), the right-leg trajectory changes sharply around the kick, while in Banana Cabinet (Fig. 10b), the traces vary across the pick, place, and push phases. In both plots, solid curves show measured joint positions and dashed curves show the corresponding action commands for the left and right sides, illustrating the task-dependent motion captured in the demonstrations. We store the demonstrations in a LeRobot v2.1 (Cadene et al., 2026)-compatible format, extended with Kimodo-specific motion and control fields for policy training with a motion prior. 847 848 849 850 851 852 853 854 855 856 857 858 859 860 861 862 863 Figure 10: Real-World Data Collection and Motion Profiles. Left: PICO-based whole-body teleoperation of the humanoid. Right: measured (solid) and commanded (dashed) left- and right- side mean joint positions for two of the eight physical-robot tasks: (a) Football Scoring, showing a pronounced right-leg change during the kick, and (b) Banana Cabinet, showing motion across the pick, place, and push phases. 16 Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027 864 865 866 867 868 869 870 871 872 873 874 875 876 877 878 879 880 881 882 883 884 885 886 887 888 889 890 891 892 893 894 Implementation Details. We fine-tune all policies with bfloat16 precision on four GPUs using 30 Hz motion sequences, a 100-frame history, and a 50-frame prediction horizon. HumanoidArena single-task policies use a global batch size of 64 for 200k steps, while the joint seven-task policy uses a batch size of 128 for 500k steps; SIMPLE uses a batch size of 64 for 200k steps, and real-world policies use a batch size of 32 for 50k steps. Scratch-trained and VLA-pretrained variants share the same fine-tuning setup and differ only in initialization. The four-layer ControlNet detaches the root-control input to body prediction. We train with an MSE objective weighted 4, 1, 1, and 0.2 for root motion, body motion, hand control, and hand transitions, respectively, using AdamW (weight decay 0.01) and a cosine schedule with 1% warm-up and a 10% minimum learning-rate ratio. The ControlNet backbone, adapters, and hand head use learning rates of 3 × 10 −5 , 1 × 10 −4 , and 1 × 10 −4 for HumanoidArena and real-world fine-tuning, and 1 × 10 −5 , 3 × 10 −5 , and 3 × 10 −5 for SIMPLE. SIMPLE training uses color jitter and continuous hand-control targets; real-world training uses color jitter and random crops, with binary hand commands conditioned on measured hand closure. At inference, all policies run on one NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 10 diffusion denoising steps and predict a 50-frame action horizon at 30 Hz. We execute 15 predicted frames per policy update on HumanoidArena and the real robot, and either 15 or 50 frames on SIMPLE depending on the evaluation setting. The SONIC tracker runs at 50 Hz; real-time correction (RTC) (Black et al., 2025c) is enabled only for real-world deployment and disabled for HumanoidArena and SIMPLE. D E XTENDED M OTION -P RIOR T RANSFER A NALYSIS Table 4 compares Kimodo-G1-SEED-v1 and RP-v1 under the same policy architecture, adaptation procedure, and HumanoidArena evaluation protocol. Both backbones contain 282M parameters, but use different motion corpora: 288 h of BONES-SEED and 700 h of Rigplay, respectively, each with a 90%/10% train/test split. Corpus composition and duration therefore change together; this comparison evaluates the choice of pretrained motion prior rather than isolating the effect of data volume. RP-v1 raises overall success from 64.29% to 67.63%, a 3.34-percentage-point gain. Improvements occur on DoubleDesk (33.33% → 40.0%), P&Pbox (75.0% → 80.0%), OpenDoor (60.0% → 93.3%), and SitSofa (90.0% → 96.7%). Performance decreases on Football (50.0% → 35.0%), Boxing (71.67% → 66.7%), and VisNavi (70.0% → 61.7%). The largest improvement is on OpenDoor, whereas the remaining changes show that transfer is task-dependent. Thus, a motion prior that improves aggregate performance need not improve every skill. Table 4 reports task-level means and standard deviations over three seeds. These descriptive com- parisons do not establish statistical significance, particularly for smaller differences relative to the reported variability. The results support the importance of motion-prior selection for downstream control, while leaving the separate contributions of corpus scale, composition, and task coverage unresolved. E E XTENDED S CALING A NALYSIS Figure 7 examines VLA pretraining data and active policy capacity in separate controlled sweeps. The data sweep holds the architecture, SonicX7 adaptation, and evaluation fixed; the model sweep holds the pretrained T2M backbone, downstream data, optimization, and evaluation fixed. RTC is disabled in both sweeps. Data scaling. Overall success increases from 68.10% at 105 h to 69.05% at 210 h and 72.14% at 419 h. These approximately twofold increases in data yield successive gains of 0.95 and 3.09 percentage points, totaling 4.04 points. The larger gain in the second interval indicates that additional pretraining data remains beneficial over the tested range. Three operating points, however, do not establish a general scaling law or predict gains beyond 419 h. Model scaling. Increasing active policy parameters from 53.6M to 91.7M improves overall success from 61.43% to 67.63% (+6.20 points); increasing to 158.9M yields 68.57% (+0.94 points). The total gain is 7.14 points, with a smaller marginal improvement over the second interval despite a larger parameter increase. This pattern supports increasing policy capacity within the tested range, while suggesting diminishing returns over the sampled sizes. It does not establish a saturation point. Because the two sweeps vary different factors, their gains should be interpreted separately; they do not establish the benefit of jointly scaling data and capacity. F E XTENDED A BLATION A NALYSIS All variants train on mixed HumanoidArena tasks in SONIC X7 and evaluate on DoubleDesk, Foot- ball, and P&Pbox. Figure 8 reports mean success across these tasks. Each component ablation is compared separately with the 51.67% baseline without VLA pretraining; the ablations are not cumulative. Motion prior and backbone freezing. Removing the pretrained T2M backbone reduces success to 18.33%, supporting its contribution to whole-body control. Separately, unfreezing the backbone 19 Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027 1026 1027 1028 1029 1030 1031 1032 1033 1034 1035 1036 1037 1038 1039 1040 1041 1042 1043 1044 1045 1046 1047 1048 1049 1050 1051 1052 1053 1054 1055 1056 1057 1058 1059 1060 1061 1062 1063 1064 1065 1066 1067 1068 1069 1070 1071 1072 1073 yields 31.67%, suggesting that preserving pretrained motion representations is beneficial under this adaptation protocol. These comparisons support retaining a frozen motion generator while learning visual and task conditioning through dedicated trainable branches. Prediction objective and gradient decoupling. Replacing MSE with Kimodo’s original motion objective yields 35.00% success, compared with 51.67% for the baseline. This favors direct super- vision of policy prediction targets while retaining the pretrained motion prior. Removing root–body gradient detachment instead yields 45.00%. Detachment preserves root-to-body conditioning but prevents the body loss from updating the root ControlNet, allowing each stage to learn through its own objective while maintaining coordinated generation. The separate comparisons support both the prediction objective and controlled cross-stage gradient flow. VLA pretraining. VLA pretraining improves success from 51.67% to 56.11%, with generally lower and less variable training loss. Both variants retain the pretrained T2M backbone, so this improve- ment indicates a complementary benefit from learning visual and task conditioning. Together, the ablations support the evaluated design choices, but do not measure interactions among simultaneous component changes or establish that their individual gains would combine additively. G L IMITATIONS AND F UTURE D IRECTIONS Limitations. A principal limitation of the current framework is its dependence on a specific low-level motion tracker. Kimodo-Policy is designed and evaluated with SONIC, and its motion- reference interface and deployment pipeline are tailored to this tracker; other tracking controllers are not currently supported. Consequently, the reported results establish the effectiveness of the policy within the SONIC-based control stack, while transfer across trackers remains unverified. Although separating high-level motion generation from low-level execution provides a modular organization, this separation alone does not ensure compatibility with controllers that differ in reference parame- terization, tracking behavior, or executable motion range. Extending the framework would therefore require adapting the policy–tracker interface and validating closed-loop performance under the target controller. Developing a more general interface between pretrained motion generation and low-level whole-body control remains an important direction for broadening its applicability. Future Work. Looking ahead, Kimodo-Policy can be viewed as a motion-prior-informed action expert within a larger multimodal architecture. Integrating it with vision–language models and video generation models, potentially through MoT-style architectures, could combine semantic un- derstanding and visual dynamics modeling with structured whole-body action generation. A com- plementary direction is to strengthen the underlying motion prior itself. Text–motion supervision can draw on human motion data retargeted to robot embodiments without requiring every sequence to be collected through robot execution with synchronized visual observations, offering a scalable route to motion pretraining. The gains observed with stronger T2M backbones motivate investi- gating whether broader motion coverage and more capable generators yield further improvements in downstream control. Beyond training robot-space motion models on retargeted data, a longer- term direction is to transfer pretrained human T2M backbones directly into humanoid VLA poli- cies, drawing on the breadth of human motion resources and advances in human motion generation. Such transfer would require aligning motion representations across embodiments and adapting hu- man kinematic priors to robot-specific actuation, balance, and contact constraints. These directions could expand the framework from a standalone policy into a reusable motion-generation component for more capable humanoid systems. 1074 1075 1076 1077 1078 1079 20
